May 12, 2025
Re: LD 1910
Senator Curry, Representative Gere, and members of the Housing and Economic Development Committee, my name is Brian Townsend, and I am the Executive Director of Commonspace. Commonspace offers programs for adults and families experiencing challenges related to homelessness, substance use, mental health, trauma, and legal system involvement in Greater Portland and Lincoln and Sagadahoc Counties. Our programs include supportive housing, housing navigation, community recovery centers, jail reentry, emergency food and shelter programs, and harm reduction and recovery programming. Commonspace is deeply engaged with the Coordinated Entry system, and is an active stakeholder within Portland's homeless response system, including holding a position on the Executive Committee of the Emergency Shelter Assessment and Response Team.
I am testifying in strong support of LD 1910, An Act to Strengthen Housing Stability Services by Increasing Support and Outreach, which will require the Department of Health and Human Services to contract with community-based nonprofit organizations to support the deployment of nine outreach case workers and nine housing stability workers statewide. This resource will provide housing and supportive services to individuals who are unhoused and chronically homeless, while simultaneously securing safe indoor environments for outreached individuals who are awaiting permanent housing. LD 1910 stipulates that this resource be distributed thoughtfully around the State, supporting all regions that have a need for these services while targeting areas with higher populations of individuals who are homeless. The bill requires ongoing appropriations of $800,000 each year for outreach case workers and $900,000 each year for housing stability workers.
As the only organization in the Portland area that provides a high-volume, low barrier day space designed to support individuals experiencing unsheltered homelessness, as well as an organization with both an active HOME Services team and Rapid Rehousing team, Commonspace has significant data and experience to weigh in on the value of this proposed resource, and to offer the strongest possible support for the passage of LD 1910. The resources created for Maine's communities and for our currently unsheltered community members by this legislation are right-sized and thoughtfully developed, and carry the promise of
www.commonspacemaine.org info@commonspacemaine.org

playing an essential role in addressing, and resolving, the surge in unsheltered homelessness across the state. This legislation would create local efforts that would target individuals with the most intractable histories of homelessness and the most significant barriers to housing, with the immediate goal of benefitting the individuals and their communities by bringing outreached clients indoors and out of unsafe outdoor living conditions, and the intersecting goal of helping these same individuals secure and sustain safe, suitable housing. It is difficult to understate how desperately our communities need this level of support. Efforts to address homelessness at the community level are challenged by many variables. But today, higher density areas such as Portland, Bangor, and Augusta are seeing and sustaining progress in finding housing for individuals who enter the shelter system. At the same time, the most vulnerable among our unhoused neighbors are living outdoors, a reality that makes housing placements exponentially more challenging. Community organizations simply do not have the resources, currently, to provide the level of outreach commitment needed to meet this challenge. It seems clear to me, as it does to the partners of Commonspace in Greater Portland and to our partners in this work across the state, that this modest investment would result in a desperately needed positive return, for our communities and for the people who are currently beyond the reach of our shelter and housing support systems. This level of contribution from the State would truly be a game-changer and would provide us with an opportunity to effectively address an issue that is challenging systems and communities across the country. LD 1910 provides an essential component of a blueprint for success that would make Maine a model for we are thoughtfully and impactfully addressing unsheltered homelessness in our state.
Sincerely,
Brian Townsend, Executive Director Commonspace

Re: LD I910, An Act to Strengthen Housing Stability Services by Increasing Support and Outreach
Senator Curry, Representative Gere, and members of the Housing and Economic Development Committee, my name is Cullen Ryan, and I am the Executive Director of Community Housing of Maine (CHOM) and serve as Chair of the
Maine Homeless Policy Committee, which assisted in creating this bill.
I am testifying in strong support of LD I910, An Act to Strengthen Housing Stability Services by Increasing Support and Outreach. This bill requires the Department ofHealth and Human Services to contract with community-based
nonprofit organizations through a request for proposals process for 9 outreach caseworkers and 9 housing stability workers. The outreach caseworkers and housing stability workers provide housing and supportive services to individuals who are unhoused and chronically homeless, as well as ensuring that the individuals are in safe indoor environments whiie awaiting permanent housing. The contracted workers are distributed around the State and targeted to areas with higher populations of individuals who are homeless. The bill requires ongoing appropriations of $800,000 each yearfor outreach caseworkers and $900,000 each yearfor housing stability workers.
This bill has the unanimous support of the Statewide Homeless Council, all three Regional Homeless Councils, and the Maine Continuum of Care. Along with funding homeless shelters, this is the top_priority of the homeless sector.
Background: Prior to 201 1, there were some 56 Intensive Case Managers (ICM) employed by DHHS serving
populations experiencing chronic homelessness in sheltered and unsheltered settings. These were a combination of
Community based ICMs and Forensic ICMs. Although ICMs worked with the same populations and their employment followed the same principles of this legislation, part of each ICM's job was to address crisis situations as they emerged around the state, drawing them away from their service to the target population. These positions were cut in the 2011 budget. Later, some Forensic ICMs were hired back, but they and Community based ICMs were never fully replenished and now the sum total stands at 24 positions statewide, with only 5 of them being Community based. This bill proposes a very focused strategy to remedy the lack of ICMs in Maine and will help us end and prevent
homelessness.
Rationale: These positions are critical because they would provide continuity of housing efforts for a population that tends to bounce through various emergency settings, so that housing efforts steadily continue no matter where the person served happens to be (shelter, jail, hospital, warming center, outside, various other shelters, etc.).
I chair the FUSE (Frequent Users System Engagement) Committee, an initiative in Portland that has been working on a by-name list effort to house people who are chronically homeless, people who are unsheltered, people who are frequent
users of emergency systems -- people in need of permanent supportive housing interventions. The group of 20 organizations has been working to end homelessness for this population for 10 years and has now housed 528 people,
and with success rates between 85 and 95% throughout the l0-year effort. Members of this Committee are experts in
their respective fields and have found that there is a correlation between the success rate once housed and the presence
of follow-up support services: when services continue to follow this population once housed their success rates have been quite high (95%); when housing stability services are lacking success rates have been markedly lower (85%). As of the end of March 2025, the success rate in housing is 85.44% - indicative of insufficient housing stability services. But the slow pace of housing is also evidence of the lack of continuity of effort. There are people on our lists that
remain unhoused after 10 years.
This Committee has also collected and analyzed jail and hospital utilization data for people who were unhoused versus people who had been housed through the initiative. This comprehensive data is quite compelling. It also demonstrates
that getting people housed creates cost savings for local, county, and state governments.
Data: As of the end of March 2025, out of the 448 people housed and still alive, not a single person was injail and 2 people were in the hospital. Out of the I44 people unhoused there were I4 people in jail and 4 people in the hospital. This means that in March, for this population, the likelihood of being in jail was infinitely higher when unhoused than when housed; and this population was more than 6 times more likely to be in the hospital when unhoused than when housed. Throughout the forty-nine (49) months this data has been collected and analyzed, it has been discovered that people who are chronically homeless are up to 29 times more likely to be in the hospital and up to 57 times more likely to be injail than when unhoused than when housed. This data is indicative of the stability that

M Maine Homeless Policy Committee
housing, coupled with adequate follow-up support services, provides. When people attain stable housing, they are exponentially less likely to interact with our overburdened and costly emergency systems. That means we save money.
It is 27 times more expensive to be in the hospital and 4 times more expensive to be in jail than in housing. The key to attaining and retaining housing for this population is housing stability and outreach case worker services.
Too often our system works in silos. As the data above shows, it is common for a person to be landing injail, the
hospital, various homeless shelters, outside in a tent or encampment, and to have contact with medical and law enforcement first responders frequently. It is extremely difficult to house someone in those circumstances. Outreach Case workers and Housing Stability workers have the sole focus sticking with a person no matter where they land in the system, maintaining the continuity of efforts to house the person, and then, importantly, working to keep them housed.
We are missing these critical positions to provide that continuity to fix the deficits of a disconnected system.
Maine's shelters are full because there is little movement into housing. Because that is a recipe for turning people away, we will continue to see an increase in unsheltered homelessness and encampments -- the worst of all outcomes.
By adding skilled services, we can empty our shelters and encampments, housing and stabilizing each person. freeing
gp capacity within our emergency shelters, and preventing encampments.
Encampments: Maine has experienced unprecedented numbers of people who are unsheltered or in encampments in recent years throughout the entire state. Maine's best strategy for moving people to safe places indoors or directly into housing from encampments is to add outreach case workers who are trained to meet people where they're at.
Data on costs of encampments: In addition to the costs borne by the State associated with homelessness and encampments, please also consider the expensive and deadly health outcomes: According to 2023 state overdose data, 73 people died of overdoses within the homeless population versus 533 who died of overdoses within the 1.395 million population of Maine. That meant that a person was 32 times more likely to die of a fatal overdose if unhoused than if housed. People are more likely to die of a fatal overdose in an encampment than they are in a supervised shelter. Encampments create other problems beyond a much higher risk of overdose, including trauma.
Encampments are miserable and hopeless places where people who do not feel good about themselves take enormous risks. People are more apathetic about living when they are in these kinds of desperate circumstances, and that affects
their decision making, and has health consequences. People are more likely to participate in risky behaviors that can
lead to contracting dangerous and potentially lifelong illnesses, such as Hepatitis C and HIV, when in an encampment
than they are in a supervised shelter.
In 2024, l4 people in the entrenched Bangor encampment contracted HIV and that same group of l4 also contracted
Hepatitis C. According to state DHHS data, it costs $30,000 for a one-time Hepatitis C treatment -- a generally
successful cure for Hepatitis C. The treatment for HIV is $36,000 annually in perpetuity. The first year of treatment alone will cost the equivalent of 6 years of housing for each person, yet instead of paying for housing, we will be
paying to keep them alive while unhoused. We will be paying for the consequences of them not being housed.
This Administration and the Legislature have made important investments in housing and ending homelessness. But
the current situation is dire, and the creation of these positions to house and keep housed this population is vital.
Please allow the system to hire these critical workers: Housing Stability Workers and Outreach Case Workers are precisely what the Statewide Homeless Council, the Maine Continuum of Care, all three Regional Homeless Councils, and the Maine Homeless Policy Committee are calling for as a priority solution to homelessness.
I implore the Legislature to pass LD l9 l0 to ensure Maine's homeless service system has outreach case workers and
housing stability workers -- currently the missing link -- to get people into housing and ensure they are successful there.
Thank you for the opportunity to comment.

Re: Support for LD1910: An Act to Strengthen Housing Stability Services by Increasing Support and Outreach
Senator Curry, Representative Gere, and the esteemed members of the Committee on Housing and Economic Development.
My name is Emily Flinkstrom and I am the Executive Director of Fair Tide, a non-profit providing deeply affordable housing and supportive services to people experiencing homelessness in the southern part of our state. I serve as a representative from Region One (York and Cumberland Counties) to the Statewide Homeless Council and am an active member of Maine's Homeless Policy Committee. Fair Tide is also the co-founder of Mainspring, a new resource hub of social services that offers coordinated, wrap-around support to help households find stability and navigate a pathway out of poverty.
In this very tough market, it is challenging to secure housing once someone falls into homelessness. The journey from homelessness to stable housing is filled with complicated applications, numerous wait lists, and loads of disappointment and frustration. Managing this process while also living in the constant crisis of not knowing where you and your family will sleep each night is nearly impossible to do alone. LD1910 will allow service providers throughout the state to offer one-on-one guidance to help folks experiencing homelessness walk through this process. The inevitable result will be a rise in successful placements into safe and secure housing.
Fair Tide's work demonstrates the critical role that these supportive services play in the housing continuum. Over our 26 years of existence, our team has been able to secure housing for hundreds of households by meeting people where they are, sitting beside them to fill out applications, advocating to landlords and offering a light at the end of a dark tunnel. We have worked with some individuals for years before finally being able to find them a home, sticking with them through the long process and connecting them to basic needs resources to keep them as safe and healthy as possible in the interim.
Just as important as the initial work of moving someone into a home is ongoing, targeted case management to ensure long-term success. Similar to other programs in our state that provide this type of support, Fair Tide has a 92% success rate in keeping folks housed for at least a year - and most for much longer. This prevents relapses into homelessness and allows individuals an opportunity to address all other aspects of life that get pushed to the side when a family is living in the crisis of homelessness. Case managers offer assistance in addressing physical and mental health issues, tackling substance use, furthering education and employment, becoming stronger parents, building a solid support system and achieving overall financial stability.
A long-term solution to homelessness

10055389:
Testimony in Support of LD 1910, An Act to Strengthen Housing Stability Services by Increasing Support and Outreach
Submitted by Jena Jones, Representative of Region III, Statewide Homeless Council
May 9, 2025
Greetings Senator Curry, Representative Gere, and members of the Housing and Economic Development Committee. My name is Jena Jones and I have the privilege of representing Region III on Maine's Statewide Homeless Council (SHC). It is the duty of the SHC to advise the Governor, the Legislature, and others on matters related to addressing, ending, and preventing homelessness. Today I write in strong support for LD 1910, An Act to Strengthen Housing Stability Services by Increasing Support and Outreach.
As the northernmost territory of the state, Region III includes all of Piscataquis, Penobscot, Hancock, Washington, and Aroostook counties. The area is geographically vast and economically diverse with sprawling rural spaces and few resource hubs. It is an area where challenges to accessing necessary resources to end one's experience of homelessness are considerable. Factors like rising poverty, few economic opportunities, the current housing crisis, shifting population dynamics, and a chronic underinvestment in mental health and substance use services are eroding the bedrock of the homeless response system, and the pipeline that is the continuum of care to access homeless services and supports has stagnated.
We have been seeing the impacts of this stagnation for some time: emergency shelter beds are full across Maine and the average number of nights folks are staying in shelter prior to exiting to housing continues to creep up. As such we see the visible effects of this imbalance of resources in the rise of unsheltered homelessness and encampments across the state as rough sleepers try to find a safe spot to stay. These folks are most often the hardest to reach given the increase in anti-camping policies that results in frequent movement as they are commonly displaced by law enforcement.
In addition to an overfull shelter system, housing subsidies, a vital component of ending someone's experience of homelessness, are infrequently available, if at all. Further compounding the issue, a shift in demographic data has revealed that more and more older adults are experiencing homelessness for the first time in their 70's, 80's, and 90's. As Maine has the oldest median age in the country, this is deeply alarming. Turmoil at the federal level adds another shade of uncertainty service providers are already experiencing. Following the end of pandemic-era supports that buoyed many

programs, providers across the state are now facing the tightening, and even shuttering, of services. Recent staggering cuts within the federal government only add to our concerns.
The challenges we currently face require such resource-intensive solutions that we are spending so much time pulling people out of the proverbial river rather than preventing them from falling in in the first place. Though not a silver bullet, LD 1910 will aid our collective ability to pull more people out of the river - and to help more folks to not fall in. One of the brightest spots in this work are the relationships built between folks experiencing homelessness and the workers helping to pull people out of the river.
Accessing the homeless services continuum can be a daunting maze to navigate - more so if you're also experiencing barriers like mental health or substance use challenges. For many, the experience of homelessness is a relatively brief and singular event - but for people experiencing chronic homelessness, for a year or more, overcoming that experience is impossible without help. The people providing that help, the outreach and housing workers like LD 1910 would provide, hold hope for the people they guide to safer, more stable spaces.
One of the biggest challenges someone experiencing homelessness in Maine right now faces is connecting to the worker who will act as that guide - particularly as many people who are chronically unhoused require solutions that meet them where they are. LD 1910 will increase the opportunity for those connections to hope and positive change at a time when it is desperately needed. The trusted relationships built between someone who is unhoused and the workers who support them are the vehicles that end homelessness - all of the important work is done in that space. Within that bond skills are built that help an individual create lasting changes and prevent recurrences of homelessness.
I implore you to aid our collective ability to meaningfully impact homelessness by voting in favor of LD 1910. This is another tool in the box at a time when investment in proven solutions is required. Thank you for your consideration.
193111:
Testimony in Support of LD 1910, An Act to Strengthen Housing Stability Services by Increasing Support and Outreach
Good afternoon, Senator Curry, Representative Gere, and the esteemed members of the Committee on Housing and Economic Development.
Thank you for the opportunity to testify today, My name is Jennifer Weatherbee, and I am the Hub
Coordinator representing -Hub 7 which covers Penobscot/Piscataquis Counties within Maine's
Homeless Response System. lam hereto express my strong support of LD 1910, An Act to
Strengthen Housing Stability Services by Increasing Support and Outreach.
Maine is facing a severe homelessness crisis. Shelters are overwhelmed, and too many people are
living outside with few options. We lack- not only housing- but people working on the ground.
Skilled and compassionate workers who can connect members of our communities who are experiencing homelessness to stable housing and walk them through these complex systems to
find housing, and to ensure- once they are housed, they are connected to the services and programs, they will need to remain successfully housed.
That's why LD 1910 is so importantli This bill addresses the gap by funding 9 outreach workersl and
9 housing stability workers across the state. These workers can provide trauma-informed care, crisis intervention, as well as connecting to needed programs and services.
These would be skilled workers who can meet people where they are--on the streets, in encampments, or public spaces--rather than referring them to office-based services that many struggle to access. Many individuals experiencing homelessness feel abandoned or mistreated by
transitional systems. We need problem solvers on the ground who are experts in housing,
healthcare, and social services.
Early engagement is built on trust and flexibility. This approach removes common barriers such as
transportation and appointment scheduling that can prevent many from accessing mainstream services. Once they have built trust, they can start the work using compassionate, trauma informed approaches and can over time transition clients into more structured and mainstream
support systems.
I stand here in my current role as the Hub Coordinator of Penobscot/Piscataquis County, but before this- I was an outreach worker. I would like to share a couple of examples of my own experiences, as well as other outreach workers- past and present. These are some of our success stories.
My first example is a chronically homeless client who was minimally known to our system. Due to Mental health and transportation issues, he remained homeless over many years and had difficulty
maintaining mainstream services. Outreach providers were able to provide swift support and help this individual get into shelter, set up with a Primary Care Provider, a housing voucher and was ultimately housed. This client was set up with long term Case Management services and continues to be housed to this day.
in a rural Washington County, an outreach worker met a man living in an abandoned trailerwith no
heat or running water. Through repeated visits, the worker gained trust, helped the individual apply

for General assistance, connected him to behavioral health services, and ultimately placed him in stable housing. With out support that could meet him on the ground, this individualwould have remained isolated and at severe risk.
One Veteran was living in a tent for over two years but refused all services and shelter, He reported that he was a veteran, but it was not verified. Over several months the outreach worker-built rapport with this client and built trust. This outreach worker went down every avenue with this client and was able to find his records and supported him with getting benefits, services and eventually stable
housing.
These stories are only a few examples of how outreach can provide hands on, on the ground support to those experiencing homelessness. People experiencing homelessness face enormous
barriers to accessing traditional services. They need consistent, community-based support. Not support in an office setting with multiple barriers to meet.
i urge this committee to pass LD 1910. It is critical step towards a more effective, humane and
stable approach to homelessness in Maine.
Thank you for time
10055351:
Testimony in Support of LD 1910: An Act to Strengthen Housing Stability Services by Increasing Support and Outreach Presented to the Joint Standing Committee on Housing and Economic Development Committee Noelle Coyne CEO, Western Maine Community Action May 12, 2025
Senator Curry Senator Bailey and Senator Bennett - distinguished members of the Housing and Economic Development Committee,
My name is Noelle Coyne, and I am writing today to express my strong support for LD 1910: An Act to Strengthen Housing Stability Services by Increasing Support and Outreach.
Maine's homelessness crisis has reached a tipping point. Shelters across the state are full or overflowing. Communities are seeing unprecedented numbers of people who are unsheltered or living in encampments, often for extended periods. What we're witnessing is not just a housing shortage, but a breakdown in the systems that are meant to help people move from crisis to stability.
LD 1910 addresses this head-on by funding 9 outreach caseworkers and 9 housing stability workers, trained, community-based professionals who are urgently needed to connect people to housing and support services. These workers will be strategically distributed across the state, focusing on areas with the greatest need.
This bill is more than a staffing proposal. It is a blueprint for system repair and recovery. Right now, people experiencing homelessness interact with multiple fragmented systems - emergency rooms, jails, shelters, with little coordination or follow-through. LD 1910 ensures that skilled professionals can provide continuity of care, helping people navigate complex systems and stay on the path to housing.
These roles are exactly what the Statewide Homeless Council, the Maine Continuum of Care, and the Maine Homeless Policy Committee have called for. They are essential for unblocking our clogged homeless response system, where shelters remain full because there are too few workers to help people move on to permanent housing.
Housing Stability Workers do more than secure a roof over someone's head,they help people stay housed. Through relationship-building and trust, they provide the kind of consistent, individualized support that is often missing for people who have experienced long-term homelessness.
Outreach Caseworkers meet people where they are quite literally. Whether in a tent encampment, under a bridge, or at a warming center, they connect individuals to health care, housing programs, and other essential supports. Without this front-line engagement, many people remain invisible to the system.

Maine's homeless response system is missing these essential positions to provide continuity and correct the deficits of a disconnected system. The efficiencies created by these positions will also inevitably pay financial dividends.
Maine's shelters are full because there is little movement into housing. When shelters are full, they often
have no choice but to turn vulnerable people away. This leads to increases in unsheltered homelessness
and encampments --- the worst of all outcomes for everyone. By adding skilled services, Maine can work
to empty its shelters and encampments, housing and stabilizing each person, freeing up capacity within our emergency shelters, and preventing encampments.
Maine has experienced unprecedented numbers of people who are unsheltered or in encampments in recent years throughout the entire state. Our state's best strategy for moving people to safe places indoors or directly into housing from encampments is to add outreach case workers who are trained to meet people where they're at to solve their homelessness. And Maine cannot afford the consequences and cost
of continued encampments.
In addition to the costs borne by the State associated with homelessness and encampments, we must also
consider the expensive and deadly health outcomes: According to 2023 state overdose data, 73 people
died of overdoses Within the homeless population versus 533 who died of overdoses within the 1.395
million population of Maine. That meant that a person was 32 times more likely to die of a fatal overdose if unhoused than if housed. People are more likely to die of a fatal overdose in an encampment than they
are in a supervised shelter. Encampments create other problems beyond a much higher risk of overdose,
including trauma.

Encampments are desolate, hopeless places where people who do not feel good about themselves take enormous risks. People are more apathetic about living when they are in these kinds of desperate
circumstances, and that affects their decision-making and has health consequences. People are more likely to participate in risky behaviors that can lead to contracting dangerous and potentially lifelong
illnesses, such as Hepatitis C and HIV, when in an encampment than they are in a supervised shelter.
In 2024, l4 people in the entrenched Bangor encampment contracted HIV, and that same group of 14
also contracted Hepatitis C. According to state DHHS data, it costs $3 0,000 for a one-time Hepatitis C

perpetuity. The first year of treatment alone will cost the equivalent of 6 years of housing for each person,

I implore this Committee and the Legislature to enact LD l9l0 to ensure Maine's homeless service
system has outreach case workers and housing stability workers -- currently the missing link -- to get
people into housing and ensure they are successful there. Maine cannot afford the financial and human

RE: Testimony in support of LD 1910 - An Act to Strengthen Housing Stability Services by Increasing Support and Outreach
Dear Senator Curry, Representative Gere & Honorable Members of the Committee on Housing & Economic Development:
My name is Richard A. Hooks Wayman, and I am a resident of Portland, Maine. I have the honor of serving as appointed Chair of Maine's Statewide Homeless Council. I also serve as the President & CEO for VOA Northern New England which is headquartered in Brunswick. VOA Northern New England is a faith-based, community nonprofit that works with people experiencing deep poverty, disabilities, and homelessness.
On behalf of the Statewide Homeless Council, I wish to submit this written testimony in support of LD 1910 an Act to strengthen housing stability services and outreach. Our state's homeless response system is fragile and insufficiently resourced to serve all families and individuals experiencing homelessness. Too many people remain stuck in our state's high quality emergency shelters awaiting a housing unit or sleep outside, in vehicles, or in structures that are not safe or habitable. While there is a spectrum of emergency shelters, transitional housing, and supportive housing, the need is simply not adequate.
Ending homelessness requires the ability to build trusting relationships with persons experiencing the trauma of homelessness and the capacity to connect people with community resources and local housing units. Maine lacks the social service capacity to work with those on our streets or in shelters. The Statewide Homeless Council unanimously supported LD 1910 as a priority policy legislation this year given the significant lack of mobile support services - the type of services that research has shown to prevent homelessness, respond to public health and law enforcement needs, locate local housing units, and achieve housing stability. Without this missing piece of our `response system' too many families and people will remain too long in shelter beds or in public encampments. This policy proposal also has a bonus of improving coordination or efficient delivery of mobile social supports by allowing the Department of Health and Human Services to contract with experienced nonprofit organizations to offer these services.
Without this incremental annual investment of $1.7 million, the Statewide Homeless Council believes that historical investments in emergency shelters, housing assistance, and housing first will not be adequately coordinated or utilized.
Thank you for considering my testimony. I am grateful for your public service and leadership to Maine!
